newsitem.title: FRANCE: France bids to end blockades with hours decree.
newsitem.headline: France bids to end blockades with hours decree.

text.p: French junior transport minister Anne-Marie Idrac said on Friday the government will sign a decree defining working hours for truckers in a bid to end a crippling truckers blockade now in its twelfth day.

Although employers and unions are due to meet at 9.30 a.m. (0830 GMT) to ratify accords on early retirement and working conditions reached on Thursday before talks broke down, drivers are maintaining their strike in a bid for wage hikes.
"The impact on citizens and on the economy is becoming dramatic in certain areas," Idrac told Europe-1 radio.
The dispute has blocked 240 main roads, closed almost half the country's petrol depots, and sent shockwaves across Europe's economies.
The deals to be signed on Friday include a pledge on payment for all working hours including time spent loading trucks.

"But people have said for years that the issue (of working hours) must be settled and we need to go further. We must clarify in an irrefutable manner what working hours should involve, what should be paid for. We need a decree," Idrac said.

She said the government would need up to 15 days to draw up the decree because the issues were complex and it had to consult the parties. "During those 15 days the blockades must be lifted. The decision to sign this decree has been taken," she said.
Truckers say they often work more than 200 hours a month, with many hours unpaid as they wait to load and unload.

But Idrac insisted pay was an issue for unions and bosses and not for the government. Unions demand pay hikes of an average 23 percent. Employers have offered a one percent real pay rise and a 1,500 franc ($300) one-time bonus.
"I think (the blockade) will go on for a while," said Roger Poletti of the Force Ouvriere (FO) union.
Yet unions also said they were willing to resume negotiations, and bosses said that while they could not increase their offer, they would be flexible in re-arranging its terms.
Employers' spokesman Rene Petit said raising the pay offer would ruin many haulage companies.

Transport Minister Bernard Pons Pons said "very positive results were obtained" before the talks broke down over pay, including the right for truckers to retire at 55 after 25 years at the wheel, changes on sick pay and travel expenses, and a ban on trucks driving at weekends.

In southern Corsica, truckers and haulage bosses conducting separate negotiations agreed overnight on a monthly wage hike of 580 francs ($116). Truckers lifted a blockade of Ajaccio's main petrol depot on Friday.
The strike, in the crucial pre-Christmas commercial period, has cost European food and haulage industries tens of millions of dollars a day, prompting protests from France's neighbours.

Prime Minister Alain Juppe ruled out using force to clear the barricades around 150 fuel depots and the country's 13 oil refineries. Petrol rationing has spread and about 5,000 of 18,000 petrol stations were either dry or feeling shortages.
The roadblocks have forced the closures of some factories for lack of supplies and cut deliveries of perishable goods ranging from fish to fruit and flowers.
